consensus_summary: Consensus primary meaning is the extreme anguish, despair, and remorse of those condemned/excluded from God's kingdom at eschatological judgment (often as conscious suffering in hell), with the fixed phrase 'weeping and gnashing of teeth'; rage/defiant anger drawn from OT/Acts usage is a widely noted alternative, alongside minority annihilationist, preterist, and purely idiomatic readings.
book_summary: The rage of the wicked at the righteous, especially when they see the kingdom from which they are excluded; their grief, hatred, gnashing, and destruction follow the pattern of the Psalms and Stephen's accusers (explicitly distinguishing this from the common teaching of anguish under everlasting torment).
consensus_core_identification: Anguish/despair/remorse of the eschatologically condemned and excluded
book_core_identification: Rage/hatred of the wicked at the righteous upon seeing their exclusion from the kingdom (Psalms/Stephen pattern, with destruction)
boundary_disagreement: Book narrows the dominant emotion from consensus primary (anguish/remorse, possibly with rage secondary) to rage/hatred as central, reorients around the Psalms/Acts hostility pattern plus destruction/melting away, and sets aside everlasting-torment anguish as merely the 'commonly taught' view rather than the symbol's core.
material_contradiction: None on the shared judgment-exclusion scenes themselves; the divergence is definitional emphasis (rage-pattern + destruction vs. primary anguish of the damned) rather than outright denial that the phrase occurs in those texts.
rationale: Minimum cores share the same NT exclusion/judgment occasions but are not equivalent: consensus centers anguish of the condemned (rage as alternative), while the book centers rage at the righteous per Psalms/Stephen and pairs it with destruction. This preserves the general referent/category (reaction of the excluded wicked) yet materially tightens emotion, intertextual pattern, and outcome, yielding refinement by reclassification at the boundary rather than wholesale replacement of the referent or pure novelty.
strongest_objection: The NT's repeated fixed collocation with 'weeping' in outer-darkness/furnace contexts more naturally signals comprehensive eschatological misery/anguish than a specialized transfer of the OT/Acts rage idiom, so elevating rage + destruction under-reads the Matthean formula.
